# Pruning apple trees

## The trees

Four trees at the bottom of the cottage garden, and the old one on the allotment boundary.

- 'Ashmead's Kernel', planted 2009, half standard on MM106
- 'Devonshire Quarrenden', planted 2011, the early red one, always the first to go over
- 'Sunset', planted 2011, small and well behaved
- 'Tom Putt', planted 2016, a cider and cooking apple from Thornhayes Nursery, £28.50 then
- The Bramley on plot 14, probably 60 years old, nobody knows who planted it

## When

Winter pruning while dormant, between leaf fall and bud burst. This year I did the garden trees on 11 and 12 January 2025 and the Bramley on 19 January. Dry, 4°C, no frost. Never in hard frost, the wood tears.

Summer pruning for the 'Sunset' only, in late August, as it's trained as a sort of goblet against the wall.

## Tools

- Felco No. 2 secateurs, bought 1994, still going. Sharpened before each session on the diamond card, same method as for the kitchen knives in [[Knife sharpening]]
- Silky Gomtaro 240 mm pruning saw
- Long-handled loppers for anything between 2 and 4 cm
- Bucket of Jeyes Fluid solution for wiping blades between trees, especially after the canker on the Bramley

## The rules I keep to

### The three Ds

Dead, damaged, diseased wood out first, all of it, before you even think about shape.

### Then crossing and rubbing

Any two branches rubbing, take the weaker or the inward one. Open the middle so a pigeon could fly through (my old head teacher's phrase, Mr Ellacott, who grew prize 'Cox' in his school garden).

### No more than a quarter

Never take more than about 20 to 25% of the canopy in one winter. If you do, the tree throws up a forest of water shoots in spring and you're worse off than before. Learned this on the Bramley in 2022 when I got carried away. 2023 it was a hedgehog of shoots.

### Tip bearers and spur bearers

'Ashmead's Kernel' and 'Sunset' are spur bearers: shorten the leaders by a third, cut laterals back to 4 or 5 buds. 'Tom Putt' fruits partly on the tips so leave most of the one-year shoots alone and only thin.

## The Bramley

### Canker

Sunken, cracked patches on two of the main limbs, the classic target-shaped rings. Cut back to clean wood about 10 cm below the visible damage. One limb, the one over the path, had to come off completely: 14 cm across at the cut. Sawed it in three goes so it didn't tear the bark. The wood went to Colin Prowse's wood burner.

### Water shoots

Took out 37 of them, I counted. Left five well-placed ones to become new fruiting wood.

## Results from last year

2024 crop, weighed on the kitchen scales:

- 'Ashmead's Kernel': 19 kg
- 'Devonshire Quarrenden': 11 kg (half the crop lost to codling moth)
- 'Sunset': 8 kg
- 'Tom Putt': 23 kg, all juiced at the community press at Lustleigh, 14 litres
- Bramley: about 70 kg, gave most away

The bees work the blossom hard in late April, and I fancy the honey from that fortnight is lighter, though that's not science. Notes on that in [[Honey extraction day]].

## After pruning

Prunings shredded for the browns in the [[Compost pile]], except the cankered ones, which are burnt. Mulched the base of each tree with 5 cm of compost, keeping it a hand's width off the trunk. Grease bands on 1 October for winter moth, off again in April.
